area_title: Origin / preflight basics / ASP.NET CORS use-cases
what_area_is_about: what a browser origin is: scheme + host + port, and how that differs from path/query/fragment
when the browser sends CORS preflight and what Access-Control-Request-Method / Access-Control-Request-Headers mean
difference between safelisted request headers and response headers JavaScript is allowed to read
what successful vs rejected preflight looks like from the browser perspective
credentialed CORS and why exact server approval is needed
ASP.NET development patterns: proxy to keep one visible origin, manual CORS policy setup, exposing Content-Disposition, and avoiding login redirects for API calls
key_ideas: CORS is enforced by browsers to protect user data; it does not protect servers from non-browser clients or malicious servers.
Origin is scheme + host + port; path and query are not part of the origin comparison.
Preflight asks permission before the real request when method/headers/content type are not safelisted.
A successful preflight does not return application data; it only permits the browser to send/read the subsequent actual request under the approved CORS constraints.
For credentialed requests, both client and server must opt in; wildcard-style permissive CORS is not enough for cookies/auth credentials.
In ASP.NET SPA development, using one browser-visible origin through proxying avoids many accidental CORS/redirect problems.
If an API request is redirected to a login page, the browser may report a CORS-like failure; API paths should usually return 401/403 instead of page redirects.
